sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Infection with an intracellular pathogen is expected to challenge the metabolic capacity of its host cell. Here, we showed that infection of epithelial cells by C. trachomatis caused global protein hypermethylation late in infection, including hypermethylation of histone lysine residues. We provided evidence that histone hypermethylation resulted from the proliferation of bacteria and that low level of activity of host demethylases accounted for this phenomenon. Further investigation of the consequences of histone hypermethylation on the host response to infection drew a complex gene-dependent picture, in line with the observation that hypermethylation led to histone modifications associated with active transcription as much as to histone modifications associated with chromatin silencing. Finally, we provide some initial evidence that drugs targeting the epigenome of the host can alter the outcome of infection in vivo.

Hypermethylation of several histone residues during C. trachomatis infection was previously documented at the cell population level (Chumduri et al., 2013). Our analysis by immunofluorescence showed cell-to-cell variability and combinatorial staining for different modifications revealed that cells that displayed a high methylation level for a given lysine also displayed hypermethylation for other residues. Hypermethylation occurred late in infection, was most prominent in cells with a high bacterial load, and was prevented by antibiotic treatment, indicating that it was linked to bacterial proliferation. We excluded a role for Nue, the predicted histone methyltransferase of C. trachomatis, as hypermethylation was also observed in cells infected by a mutant strain that did not express Nue. A proteomic analysis of infected cells showed that, in addition to histones, several proteins were hypermethylated, consistent with the observation that histone demethylases have multiple substrates (Kuwik et al., 2023). Hypermethylated proteins include several implicated in mRNA synthesis and processing, with potential consequences on host gene expression. Hypermethylation also occurred on cytoplasmic proteins, such as tubulin or keratin 18. For the latter, the possibility of methylation at the site we identified had already been reported (Jang et al., 2019).

The hypermethylation of histones and its correlation with bacterial burden suggested that infection might create an environment favoring methylation reaction over demethylation. Consistent with this premise, we observed that infected cells were sensitized to the histone demethylase inhibitor JIB-04, indicating that demethylase activity is low late in infection. This was confirmed by directly measuring one such activity (on H3K4me3) in nuclei extracts isolated from infected cells. The strong loss of activity (75% reduction at 40 hpi) suggests that the reduction in KDM enzymatic activity may affect a larger proportion of cells than detected with antibodies against histone methylation marks, possibly because of low SAM availability (see below). Several observations support the hypothesis that the metabolic burden of infection is responsible for the global histone hypermethylation (i) histone hypermethylation increased with infection time and positively correlated with bacterial load; (ii) antibiotic treatment reduced histone hypermethylation (iii) histone hypermethylation was partially abolished by providing aKG or Fe(II), cofactors for demethylases of the Jumonji family; and (iv) succinate concentration, a competitor for aKG, doubled in the nuclei of infected cells. Altogether, these data strongly suggest that aKG and Fe(II) become limiting during late infection. Indeed, Fe(II) is captured from the host cytoplasm by the bacteria (Pokorzynski et al., 2017). The host responds by enhancing expression of the transferrin receptor (3.3-fold increase of the transcript, Supplementary files 4 fivefold increase of the protein, Supplementary file 2) but cytosolic and nuclear Fe(II) concentrations might remain at a sub-optimal concentration for demethylase activities. The second metabolite, aKG, represents an entry point into C. trachomatis incomplete Krebs cycle (Mehlitz et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 1998). A prior metabolomic study also detected a global increase in succinate levels in C. trachomatis-infected cells (Rother et al., 2018), in agreement with the twofold increase we measured in purified nuclei. The same study showed that aKG levels remained globally stable while fumarate, another competitive metabolite for aKG-dependent 2-oxoglutarate oxygenase (Xiao et al., 2012) also increased over the course of infection. Thus, an increase in the ratio of succinate and fumarate over aKG, together with low iron level, can account for the decrease in demethylase activity. In agreement with the hypothesis of limiting metabolites, replenishment of the culture medium was sufficient to partially prevent histone hypermethylation.

Is protein hypermethylation also a consequence of increased SAM availability? Measurement of SAM levels at single-cell resolution using a ratiometric probe indicated that SAM levels remained stable throughout infection. Measurement of SAM concentration in isolated nuclei suggested, if anything, a decrease in this compartment. Thus, while Chlamydia hijack SAM (Binet et al., 2011), the host appears to adapt its metabolism to maintain normal SAM levels. Importantly, our measurements revealed the heterogeneity in SAM levels in HeLa cells. Such heterogeneity was also observed in other cell lines (Dey et al., 2022). While we lack single-cell resolution for the abundance of other key metabolites (aKG, succinate/fumarate, iron) we can hypothesize that a certain level of SAM is required to sustain HMT activity, below which proteins would escape hypermethylation. In addition, more SAM might become available late in the infectious cycle, once the bacterial consumption slows down, and be immediately consumed in methylation reactions, without accumulating at detectable levels. Thus, late increase in SAM availability, or decrease in the by-product, S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), might also contribute to protein hypermethylation.

Consistent with low SAM levels in the nuclei of infected cells, we observed that DNA was slightly hypomethylated late in infection, as previously reported (Bryan et al., 2021). How can protein hypermethylation and DNA hypomethylation be reconciled, when Ten-eleven-translocation (TET) oxidative demethylases, which initiate DNA demethylation, also use aKG and iron as cofactors? Enhanced expression of GADD45A and GADD45B (3.8-fold and 2.4-fold increase in the transcripts, respectively, Supplementary file 4), which promote DNA demethylation downstream of TET enzymes, might compensate for reduced TET enzyme activity (Li et al., 2015). Also, methylation and demethylation reactions depend on the relative affinity of each enzyme for their co-factors and on their respective rates of activities (Islam et al., 2018). This, together with the difference in turnover between DNA and histone methylation/demethylation events, might contribute to the different outcomes when comparing methylation levels of DNA and histones in infection.

Epigenetic modifications govern the accessibility of chromatin. Formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements enrichment followed by sequencing (FAIRE-Seq) experiments had shown that the proportion of all differentially accessible regions mapping to promoter regions was at its highest late in Hep2 cells infected with C. trachomatis, with the majority of regions showing a reduction in chromatin accessibility (Hayward et al., 2020). Keeping in mind the caveat that ChIP-seq data were obtained on the whole cell population, when only a fraction of infected cells display histone hypermethylation, our analyzes show that, at least for H3K4 and H3K9, methylation modifications spread throughout chromatin, suggesting that hypermethylation occurs randomly. Since histone methylation can repress or activate gene transcription depending on the residue modified and its position relative to the genetic element, the overall effect histone hypermethylation might have on host gene expression was unclear. To answer this question, we examined the transcriptional changes in the host response to infection upon DMKG supplementation. Interpretation of the data calls for caution, since DMKG supply only partially prevents histone hypermethylation. In addition, hypermethylation affects several proteins involved in mRNA processing (Figure 1D) and DMKG supplementation might affect transcript levels independently of its effect on histone methylation. DMKG supplementation modified the transcription of about one third of the infection-responsive transcripts, indicating that histone hypermethylation contributes to modulating the transcriptional response of the host to infection. DMKG supply did not globally enhance or dampen the host response to infection, since a similar proportion of transcripts were differentially up- and downregulated. A discrete set of infection-regulated genes responded strongly (>2.5 fold) to DMKG supplementation, including genes involved in the MAPK signaling pathway and in cytokine signaling (Supplementary file 5). Finally, several non-coding RNAs were differentially regulated during infection, in a DMKG-sensitive manner, including several tRNAs. Modification in the activity of Fe(II)/aKG-dependent RNA demethylases might be implicated in this phenomenon, as methylations are among the post-transcriptional modifications regulating tRNA stability (Adami and Bottai, 2020). Interestingly, a drop in host protein synthesis was previously reported in Chlamydia infected cells (Ohmer et al., 2019). The decrease in tRNA levels could contribute to this phenomenon.

Our data converge to link protein hypermethylation in infection to the metabolic pressure exerted by bacterial growth. Does it benefit the host or the bacteria? The question is difficult to answer in the absence of a complex model in which protein methylation levels could be controlled experimentally. In vitro, iron supplementation reduced histone hypermethylation without affecting progeny production, indicating that hypermethylation is not required for the generation of infectious bacteria. Furthermore, it is likely that the bacteria have adapted their growth rate to limit possible deleterious consequences of the metabolic pressure they exert on the host. Interestingly, several demethylase inhibitors hindered bacterial proliferation in vitro, indicating that increasing histone methylation beyond its physiological range was deleterious for the bacteria. We tested the effect of one broad demethylase inhibitor, JIB-04, on the outcome of infection in an animal model. A reduction of bacterial burden upon exposure to JIB-04 was observed, although below statistical significance with only 6 animals per group. A trend towards reduced tissue damage was also observed, but the effect remained modest. Interpretation of these observations calls for caution, as exposition to JIB-04 might affect non-infected cells implicated in bacterial clearance. Thus, the trend to a reduction in bacterial burden and pathology might not be related to the decrease in bacterial proliferation upon treatment with demethylase inhibitors observed in vitro. Still, these data suggest that chemical modifications of the epigenome of the host can impact the outcome of infection.

In conclusion, the effect of metabolites on the epigenetic status of chromatin are documented in metabolic diseases, in cancer, and in the influence exerted by the gut microbiota on host physiology. We show here that the metabolic activity of an intracellular bacterium has the potential to compromise metabolic homeostasis of the host and to weigh on the host response to infection through epigenetic alterations.

sec.title: Cells
sec.p: HeLa cells (ATCC) and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) were grown in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium with Glutamax (DMEM, Invitrogen), supplemented with 10% (v/v) heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS). Primary epithelial cells were isolated from ectocervix biopsies of female patients after approval by the French Ethical Committee ‘CPP Ile de France 1’ on May 9, 2016. Approval and authorization of the National Data Protection Authority (‘Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés’, CNIL) have been obtained for the research protocol, in compliance with the Helsinki principles. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. Primary cells were cultivated in keratinocyte serum-free medium (KSFM, Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing 50 mg/L of bovine pituitary extract (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 5 μg/L of human recombinant epidermal growth factor (EGF) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) (Tang et al., 2021). They were used between passages 3 and 6. All cell cultures were maintained at 37 °C, in a 5% CO2 atmosphere, and were routinely tested for mycoplasma by PCR.

sec.title: Bacteria
sec.p: The C. trachomatis serovar LGV L2 strain 434 was from ATCC. For IFU measurements and for image analysis, bacteria stably transformed with a plasmid expressing the green fluorescent protein (GFP) or mCherry under the control of the incD promoter (L2IncDGFP and L2IncDmCherry) were used, respectively (Agaisse and Derré, 2013). For the experiments with organoids C. trachomatis L2 or C. muridarum CM006 expressing GFP in p2TK2 or pNigg-derived vectors, respectively, were used (Dolat and Valdivia, 2021). C. muridarum was the MoPn strain provided by Scot Ouellette (University of Nebraska). The C. trachomatis serovar LGV L2 strain 434 with an allele in nuE leading to a W71* truncation (C to T mutation at position 129786) was obtained by chemical mutagenesis as previously described (Kokes et al., 2015). The resulting rifamycin-resistant mutant CTL2M340 was back-crossed with a spectinomycin-resistant wild-type L2 strain to give rise to the CTL2M340rs59 recombinant strain (referred to here as Nue*). Nue* contains 16 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) compared to the parental strain, which are listed in Supplementary file 8. Bacteria were propagated on HeLa cells using standard procedures (Scidmore, 2005).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: Cells (50×103 per well) were seeded in a 24-well-plate on a glass coverslip and infected at MOI = 1 the following day. In some experiments, the medium was changed 24 hpi for complete medium supplemented with ferric ammonium citrate (MP Biomedicals #158040 100 mM stock), or dimethyl α-ketoglutarate (DMKG, Sigma #349631, the 7.18 M preparation was adjusted to 2.5 M stock with DMSO, aliquoted and frozen), or JIB-04 (Sigma #SML0808 5 mM frozen stock in DMSO, intermediate dilution 40 μM in culture medium), or chloramphenicol (Sigma #C0378 34 mg/ml stock in ethanol), or ciprofloxacin (Sigma 17850 0.3 mM stock in culture medium) or SD70 (Xcess Biosciences #M60194-2S, 40 mM stock in DMSO) or TACH101 (MedChemExpress #HY-O0297 and #HY-O0298 1:1, 150 μM stock in DMSO). Cells were fixed 48 hpi unless otherwise indicated in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 4% sucrose in phosphate-buffer saline (PBS) for 20 min, followed by 10 min in 50 mM NH4Cl in PBS, and then washed in PBS. Coverslips were permeabilized with 0.3% TritonX-100 in PBS for 5 min and washed in PBS. Samples were incubated for 1 hr in primary antibodies diluted in 1 mg/ml bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.01% Tween-20 in PBS, washed three times in PBS, and then incubated for 1 hr in secondary antibodies with 0.5 μg/ml 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (Invitrogen). Antibodies used are listed in Supplementary file 6. Samples were washed in PBS and then mounted on slides in Mowiol. Microscopy was performed on an Axio Observer Z1 microscope equipped with an ApoTome module (Zeiss, Germany) and a 20 X Apochromat lens. Images were taken with an ORCA-Flash4.OLT camera (Hamamatsu, Japan) using the ZEN software from Zeiss.

sec.title: Image analysis and quantification
sec.p: Image analysis was performed with Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012), the different steps described below were automatically performed using a Fiji macro script. Cell nuclei and inclusions appeared in the uv/DAPI channel (DNA stain) while only inclusions appeared in the red/mCherry channel (mCherry-expressing bacteria). A median filter of radius 2 was applied to both channels for noise removal. ‘Triangle’ and ‘Huang’ automatic threshold methods were, respectively, used on mCherry and DAPI channels to create binary masks. The mCherry mask was subtracted from the DAPI mask, resulting in a binary mask corresponding to cell nuclei. The FIJI functions ‘Erode,’ ‘Dilate,’ ‘Fill Holes,’ and ‘Watershed’ were successively applied to the resulting mask for nuclei individualization. The FIJI functions ‘Erode,’ ‘Dilate’ two times and ‘Watershed’ were successively applied to the inclusion mask to individualize inclusions and dilate them by one pixel to create an overlap with the nuclei next to inclusions. Regions of interest (ROI) corresponding to inclusions were defined on the inclusions mask using ‘Analyze Particles’ function with ‘Size’ parameter set to ‘30-Inf.’ ROI corresponding to nuclei were defined on the nuclei mask using ‘Analyze Particles’ function with ‘Size’ parameter set to ‘50–500’ and ‘Exclude on edges’ option on. For each nuclei ROI, the macro checked each inclusion ROI one by one to see if there was an overlap with the nuclei ROI. This was done by selecting the intersection of both ROI (‘AND’ function of the ROI Manager) and by checking if it was not empty (selectionType() > –1). Nuclei were considered as from an infected cell if they were overlapping with at least one inclusion. For Figure 2B, the overlap area was measured, and nuclei were associated with the inclusion they were overlapping the most with. The mean intensity in each channel was measured for each nucleus and inclusion. Finally, for each field, three composite pictures of DAPI and mCherry channels were saved, displaying either inclusions, infected, or non-infected nuclei segmentation for post-processing verification. The mean value of intensity for a given histone mark in non-infected samples was calculated. Nuclei whose intensity was greater than two times this value were counted as positive. Positive nuclei from non-infected cells were manually double-checked and corrected as nuclei from infected cells if they had been misclassified by the automated procedure.

sec.title: Organoid culture and imaging
sec.p: Murine endometrial organoids were generated as previously described from C57BL/6 J (Jackson Laboratory, strain no. 000664) (Dolat and Valdivia, 2021). Bacteria were diluted in phosphate-buffered saline to a final concentration of 5×106 IFU, vortexed for 15 s and pipetted into a borosilicate capillary glass needle. Organoids were microinjected using an Eppendorf FemtoJet 4 x at a steep vertical angle and only punctured once and refed with media containing 10 μg/mL gentamicin 1 hr after injection. At the indicated timepoint, organoids were washed with warm PBS, fixed with 3% warm paraformaldehyde for 20 min, and resuspended in 0.5 mL 0.25% ammonium chloride. Organoids were centrifuged at 600 × g for 5 min, resuspended in PBS containing 2% BSA (Fraction V; Equitech-Bio) and 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma), and incubated on a rocker at 25 °C. The organoids were centrifuged at 600 × g for 5 min and incubated with rabbit anti-H3K9me3 (1:50) overnight at 4 °C. Organoids were washed once with 2% BSA, centrifuged at 600 × g for 5 min, and incubated with anti-rabbit conjugated to Alex Fluor 647 (1:1000) and Hoechst (2 μg/mL) for 1.5 hr at 25 °C. Organoids were centrifuged at 600 × g for 5 min, resuspended in Vectashield (Vector Labs; H-1000), pipetted onto a glass slide, and overlaid with a coverslip. Organoids (nine organoids for infections with C. trachomatis and seven for C. muridarum) were imaged using an inverted microscope (TI2-E; Nikon Instruments) equipped with an ORCA Flash 4.0 V3 sCMOS camera (Hamamatsu), SOLA solid-state white illumination (Lumencor), and acquired using a 20 x Plan Apochromatic NA 0.75 air objective with the NIS-Elements Software (Nikon). 3D reconstructions were generated in ImageJ (NIH) and the nuclei were segmented using auto local thresholding and the watershed algorithm. The mean intensity in infected cells and neighboring, uninfected cells was measured, plotted, and analyzed in RStudio. Statistical analysis was performed using a Welch’s t-test.

sec.title: Proteomic analyses
sec.p: 35 mm dishes were plated with 400,000 HeLa cells and infected or not the following day with C. trachomatis L2 at MOI = 2. Forty-eight hours later, the cells were collected and resuspended in Tris 100 mM, 8 M urea pH 7.5. Biological triplicates were prepared. Proteins were reduced using 5 mM TCEP for 30 min at room temperature. Alkylation of the reduced disulfide bridges was performed using 10 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. Proteins were then digested in two steps: first with 1 µg r-LysC Mass Spec Grade (Promega) for 4 hr at 30 °C and then samples were diluted to 1.8 M urea with 100 mM Tris HCl pH 8.5 and 1 µg Sequencing Grade Modified Trypsin was added for the second digestion overnight at 37 °C. Proteolysis was stopped by adding formic acid (FA) at a final concentration of 5%. The resulting peptides were desalted on a Stage Tip (Rappsilber et al., 2007) prepared with Empore 3M C18 material (Fisher Scientific). Peptides were eluted using 50% acetonitrile (ACN), and 0.1% formic acid (FA). Peptides were concentrated to dryness and resuspended in 2% ACN/0.1% FA just prior to LC-MS injection.

LC-MS/MS analysis was performed on a Q Exactive Plus Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with a Proxeon EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). One µg of peptides was injected onto a home-made 32 cm C18 column (1.9 μm particles, 100 Å pore size, ReproSil-Pur Basic C18, Dr. Maisch GmbH, Ammerbuch-Entringen, Germany). Column equilibration and peptide loading were done at 900 bars in buffer A (0.1% FA). Peptides were separated with a multi-step gradient from 3 to 6% buffer B (80% ACN, 0.1% FA) in 5 min, 6 to 31% buffer B in 130 min, and 31 to 62% buffer B in 30 min at a flow rate of 250 nL/min. Column temperature was set to 60 °C. MS data were acquired using Xcalibur software using a data-dependent method. MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 70,000 and MS/MS scans (fixed first mass 100 m/z) at a resolution of 17,500. The AGC target and maximum injection time for the survey scans and the MS/MS scans were set to 3E6, 20 ms and 1E6, 60 ms, respectively. An automatic selection of the 10 most intense precursor ions was activated (Top 10) with a 30 s dynamic exclusion. The isolation window was set to 1.6 m/z and normalized collision energy was fixed at 27 for HCD fragmentation. We used an underfill ratio of 1.0% corresponding to an intensity threshold of 1.7E5. Unassigned precursor ion charge states as well as 1, 7, 8, and >8 charged states were rejected, and peptide match was disabled.

sec.title: Protein identification
sec.p: Acquired Raw data were analyzed using MaxQuant software version 1.6.6.0 using the Andromeda search engine (Tyanova et al., 2016). The MS/MS spectra were searched against the Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2-434-Bu and the Homo sapiens UniProt reference proteome database (884 and 79,057 entries, respectively). All searches were performed with oxidation of methionine, mono- and di-methylation of lysine and arginine, trimethylation of lysine, and acetylation of lysine and protein N-terminus as variable modifications and cysteine carbamidomethylation as fixed modification. Trypsin was selected as protease allowing for up to two missed cleavages. The minimum peptide length was set to five amino acids and the peptide mass was limited to a maximum of 8000 Da. One unique peptide to the protein group was required for the protein identification. The main search peptide tolerance was set to 4.5 ppm and to 20 ppm for the MS/MS match tolerance. Second peptides were enabled to identify co-fragmentation events and match between runs option was selected with a match time window of 0.7 min over an alignment time window of 20 min. The false discovery rate (FDR) for peptide and protein identification was set to 0.01. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD051857.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis of proteomics data was based on the comparison of intensities between biological conditions. Proteins identified as reverse hits or potential contaminants were first removed from the analysis. Intensities associated with at least one unique peptide were kept for further statistics. Additionally, only proteins with at least two intensity values in one of both conditions were kept to ensure a minimum of replicability. Next, intensities were log2-transformed. They were normalized so that the intensities of human proteins are centered in each sample on the mean of the medians of the human protein intensities across all samples. This normalization was carried out to ensure that the intensities in each sample corresponded to a same global level of the host proteins. Proteins without any intensity value in one of both conditions have been considered as proteins quantitatively present in a condition and absent in the other. They have, therefore, been set aside and considered as differentially abundant proteins. Next, missing values of the remaining proteins were imputed using the impute.mle function of the R package imp4p (Gianetto et al., 2020). Statistical testing was conducted using limma t-tests thanks to the R package limma (Ritchie et al., 2015). The FDR control was performed using an adaptive Benjamini–Hochberg procedure on the resulting p-values thanks to the function adjust.p of R package cp4p using the robust method to estimate the proportion of true null hypotheses among the set of statistical tests (Giai Gianetto et al., 2016). The proteins associated to an absolute log2(fold-change) superior to 1 and adjusted p-values inferior to a FDR level of 1% have been considered as significantly differentially abundant proteins.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of modified peptides
sec.p: We searched for mono-, di-, or tri-methylations on lysine or arginine residues, or for succinylation on lysine residues. Some modifications were identified through mass differences in MS1 spectra, without precise localization on the peptide. Others have been pinpointed on their respective peptides using MS/MS spectra with localization probabilities exceeding 0.75 as determined by MaxQuant. For statistical analyses, raw intensities of all identified modified peptides in the experiments were log2-transformed. Subsequently, they were normalized by median centering within the biological conditions (infected or not infected) to account for potential shifts in peptide median signals between conditions. Missing values were then imputed by condition using the impute.mle function from the R package imp4p. Standard t-tests were employed to examine whether the fold-changes of modified peptides significantly differed from 0 between conditions. Furthermore, ANOVA contrast analyses were conducted to identify modified peptides with fold-changes significantly diffcell analyses revealed erent from those of the unmodified proteins to which they belong as explained in Giai Gianetto, 2023.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Wild-type and Nue* bacteria were lysed in urea buffer (8 M urea, 1% SDS (v/v), 150 mM NaCl, 30 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0), normalized for protein content (BCA Protein assay, Pierce) and lysates were subjected to sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane. The membrane was blocked with 1 x PBS containing 5% milk and 0.01% Tween 20. The membranes were then immunoblotted with primary antibodies diluted in the same buffer. Primary antibodies against Nue were previously described (Pennini et al., 2010). Primary antibodies against Hsp60 (GroEL) were obtained by immunizing rabbits with GroEL purified from C. muridarum, kindly provided by Lingling Chen (Illingworth et al., 2017). Secondary antibodies were anti-rabbit-HRP (Invitrogen) conjugated antibodies. Blots were developed using the Western Lightning Chemiluminescence Reagent (GE Healthcare) and imaged using Fusion FX (Vilber).

sec.title: Nuclei isolation and measure of DNA methylation
sec.p: 35 mm dishes were seeded with 4×105 HeLa cells. Cells were infected or not at MOI = 2 with C. trachomatis LGV L2. Forty-eight hpi, cells were washed in PBS and detached in PBS-EDTA, centrifuged for 5 min at 400 × g and resuspended in 344 ml of hypotonic buffer (10 mM Tris pH 7.65, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, 0.2% NP-40, 0.6 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl (PMSF), 1 X Protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma)). Volume was adjusted to about 1 ml by adding PBS, cells were then lysed using a Dounce homogenizer (20 up and down), and then 96 μl of sucrose buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.65, 15 mM KCl, 60 mM NaCl, 0.34 M sucrose, 150 mM spermine (Merck S4264), 50 mM spermidine (Merck S0266), 0.6 mM PMSF, 1 X protease inhibitor cocktail) was added to the samples. Samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 500 × g, supernatants were discarded, and the pellets were frozen. Genomic DNA was extracted with RNase A and digested with the kit nucleoside digestion mix of NEB (M0649S) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The reaction was processed for LC-MS/MS analysis. Analysis of total 5-methyl-2′-deoxycytidine (5-mdC) concentrations was performed using a Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), equipped with an electrospray ionization source (H-ESI II Probe) coupled with an Ultimate 3000 RS HPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Digested DNA was injected onto a Thermo Fisher Hypersil Gold aQ chromatography column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 1.9 µm particle size) heated at 30 °C. The flow rate was set at 0.3 mL/min and run with an isocratic eluent of 1% acetonitrile in water with 0.1% formic acid for 10 min. Parent ions were fragmented in positive ion mode with 10% normalized collision energy in parallel-reaction monitoring (PRM) mode. MS2 resolution was 17,500 with an AGC target of 2e5, a maximum injection time of 50 ms, and an isolation window of 1.0 m/z. The inclusion list contained the following masses: dC (228.1), 5-mdC (242.1). Extracted ion chromatograms of base fragments (±5 ppm) were used for detection and quantification (112.0506 Da for dC; 126.0662 Da for 5-mdC). Calibration curves were previously generated using synthetic standards in the ranges of 0.2–50 pmoles injected for dC and 0.02–10 pmoles for 5-mdC. Results are expressed as a % of total dC.

sec.title: SAM measurement in nuclei
sec.p: For each condition, a 10 cm dish was seeded with 2.5 million HeLa cells. Cells were infected or not at MOI = 2 with C. trachomatis LGV L2. Forty hpi, nuclei were isolated as described above. The samples were divided into eight aliquots and centrifuged at 500 × g for 5 min. The pellet (nuclei) was resuspended in 40 μl of CM buffer from the Mediomics Bridge-It SAM fluorescence assay (Gentaur) (2 aliquots, flash-frozen) or urea buffer (30 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, 8 M urea, 1% SDS, pH = 8.0) (1 aliquot) to determine protein concentration using a BCA protein assay kit (Pierce 23225). Aliquots were thawed and normalized to equal protein concentrations in CM buffer, diluted 1:4 in CM buffer, and incubated for 1 hr at 24 °C with vigorous shaking. Samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 16,000 × g. The supernatant was diluted 1:5 in Buffer S, mixed, and 20 μl of the mix was deposited on one Optiplate (Perkin Elmer #6005270) in duplicate. 80 μl of reaction buffer was added to each well. The reaction was incubated for 40 min at room temperature before reading fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) on a FLUOStar Omega with filters (485–12 excitation 540 nm–10 emission, 485–12 excitation 660 nm–10 emission). SAM concentrations in test samples were then determined using a SAM standard curve.

sec.title: SAM measurement in living cells
sec.p: 8-well μ-slides (Ibidi #80827) were seeded with 65,000 HeLa cells per well. On the following day, cells were transfected with pAV-U6+27-Tornado-F30-Broccoli-Squash-SAM-sensor 5–1 (Addgene #177920) and infected or not 4 hr later with L2IncDmCherry at MOI = 1. Two days later, 5 μM BI dihydrochloride (Tocris Bioscience #7466, 10 mM stock in DMSO) and 10 μM DFHO (Tocris Bioscience #6434, 10 mM stock in DMSO) were added to the wells. In one control well, 20 mM cycloleucine (Sigma #A48105) was added. Cells were imaged 1 hr later (corresponding to 40 hpi) with a STELLARIS 8 inverted microscope (Leica Microsystems, Mannheim, Germany). A supercontinuum white light laser tunable between 440 and 790 nm was used for excitation and focused through an HC PL APO CS2 40 x, NA 1.2 motCORR water immersion objective. Emission signals were captured with Power HyD S and X detectors. The system was controlled with Leica Application Suite (LAS) X. The excitation wavelength and detection window are the following: DAPI (405 nm; 415–450 nm), Broccoli (460 nm; 475–507 nm); Squash (512 nm; 517–555 nm); and mCherry (587 nm; 598–683 nm). All segmentations were performed using the pretrained Cellpose v2.2.3 model (cyto) with the diameter parameter set to 0. Cells were segmented based on the CellTracker Blue signal, whereas inclusions were segmented from the mCherry channel. The workflow described below was performed semi-automatically using a custom Fiji macro. Regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to cells and inclusions were generated from the Cellpose masks. Only ROIs corresponding to transfected cells were retained for further analysis and were manually corrected when necessary. Nuclei were segmented as follows. Both the cytoplasm and nuclei were visible in the Broccoli channel, whereas only the cytoplasm was detected in the Squash channel. The Broccoli image was divided by the Squash image to generate a new image in which nuclei were specifically highlighted. A Gaussian blur filter (σ=2) was applied, and a threshold was manually adjusted for each cell to segment its nucleus (or nuclei). To identify infected cells, each cell ROI was sequentially compared with all inclusion ROIs to determine overlap. When a cell overlapped multiple inclusions, it was assigned to the inclusion with the largest overlap area. For each cell, the integrated fluorescence intensities in the Broccoli and Squash channels were measured separately in the nuclei and cytoplasm. For each inclusion, the integrated mCherry fluorescence intensity and area were measured. Broccoli-to-Squash fluorescence intensity ratios were calculated and correlated with inclusion-associated mCherry fluorescence intensities. Data visualization and statistical analyses were performed in RStudio. Differences in fluorescence ratios were assessed using Welch’s t-test, and correlations were evaluated using Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r).

sec.title: H3K4me3 demethylation activity and succinate measurement
sec.p: Ten centimeter dishes were seeded with 1.5 million HeLa cells (2 dishes were used for the infected plates, to compensate for a lower nucleus harvest). Cells were infected or not at MOI = 2 with C. trachomatis LGV L2. Forty hpi, nuclei were isolated as described above and resuspended in 0.3 ml of ice-cold PBS with 1 X Protease inhibitor cocktail. Samples were sonicated three times for 5 s with cooling on ice between sonication steps and centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000 × g at 4 °C. The supernatants were collected and centrifuged a second time for 5 min. The supernatants were immediately used to measure their ability to demethylate H3K4me3 by immune-detection of the reaction product using the Epigentek kit P-3083. Briefly, 5 μl of nuclear extracts was mixed to 45 ul of the manufacturer’s assay buffer JD2 supplemented with 2 μM ascorbate, loaded onto a plate coated with H3K4me3, and incubated for 120 min at 37 °C. The demethylated products were revealed with a specific antibody following the manufacturer’s instructions and fluorometrically measured on a plate reader (Tecan) at 530 nm excitation and 590 nm emission. Background readings were given by heat inactivation of the nuclear extracts prior to the demethylase reaction (15 min at 85 °C). The remainder of the nuclear extracts were flash-frozen and later used to determine protein and succinate concentrations using BCA and Succinate-Glo JmjC Demethylase/Hydroxylase (Promega V7990) assay kits, respectively. Nuclear extracts were heat-inactivated prior to succinate measurement; samples were diluted 1:10 and 25 μL were used. Protein concentrations were used to normalize H3K4me3 demethylase activity and succinate concentrations in nuclear extracts.

sec.title: Progeny assays
sec.p: HeLa cells (105) were seeded in a 24-well plate. The next day cells were infected with L2IncDGFP bacteria at an MOI = 0.15. 24 hr post infection, the medium was replaced with fresh medium supplemented with the indicated drug, or left unchanged, with the addition of DMSO in the well if the drug was dissolved in DMSO. Cells were detached 48 hpi, lysed using glass beads, and the supernatant was used to infect new HeLa cells plated the day before (100,000 cells/well in a 24-well plate), in serial dilution. The next day, three wells per condition with an infection lower than 30% (checked by microscopy) were detached and fixed as described above, before analysis by flow cytometry and determination of the bacterial titer. Acquisition was performed using a CytoFLEX S (Beckman Coulter) and 50,000 events per sample were acquired and then analyzed using FlowJo (version 10.0.7).

sec.title: Transfections
sec.p: One day after being seeded in a 24-well-plate (105 cells/well) in 500 μL of complete medium transfection mix was added to cells 50 μL of Jetprime buffer (Polyplus), 0.5 μg of DNA, and 3 μL of Jetprime transfection reagent (Polyplus) per well. After 3 hr, the medium was changed to a new complete medium containing mCherry-bacteria at MOI = 0.5. Plasmids used were coding for HA-tagged KDM4A/JMJD2A, KDM5A, and dKDM5A (H483A mutation) were obtained from Addgene (#24180, #14800 and #14801, respectively). The plasmid coding for dKDM4A was generated from the wild-type construct by restriction-free cloning (van den Ent and Löwe, 2006) using primers ctcgacggatcaattcaccat and aggtagttgatgctgtagaggtccatgtcttcagtgGCccaagcaaaggatgtcttcc. This resulted in His-to-Alanine mutation in the catalytic site (position 188).

sec.title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation
sec.p: Four 15 cm culture dishes were seeded with 6×106 cells and half were infected the day after at MOI = 2. Forty-eight hours later, cells were rinsed twice in PBS and fixed by adding 15 ml of fixation medium prewarmed to 37 °C 15 mM NaCl, 0.15 mM EDTA, 0.075 mM EGTA, 0.015 mM HEPES in DMEM pH 8.0. Formaldehyde (Sigma F-8775) was added to the prewarmed medium just prior to the fixation step to the final concentration of 1%. Cells were rocked gently at room temperature; afterwards, formaldehyde was quenched by adding glycine drop by drop from a 1.06 M stock prepared fresh to a final concentration of 0.125 M. Quenching was pursued for 5 min with gentle rocking, the cells were rinsed twice with PBS, scraped using a soft silicone scraper, and transferred to a 15 ml conical tubes on ice, pooling the two identical plates together. Cells were centrifuged at 400 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, the pellet was resuspended in 10 ml cold PBS, centrifuged again. The pellet was resuspended in 1 ml of cold PBS and centrifuged, the supernatant was discarded and the pellet was frozen at – 80 °C. Pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 140 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA (pH 8), 10% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40, 0.25% Triton X-100), and incubated for 10 min at 4 °C. After centrifugation (300 × g, 5 min, 4 °C) the supernatant was discarded, the pellet resuspended in buffer (200 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA (pH 8), 0.5 mM EGTA (pH 8), 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8)), and FPIC (Fast Protease Inhibitors Cocktail; Sigma-Aldrich; #S8830-20TAB) and incubated 10 min at 4 °C. After centrifugation the supernatant was discarded and the pellet resuspended in low-SDS buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 0.1% SDS, 0.95% NP-40, 0.1% NaDoC, 10 mM EDTA (pH 8), 150 mM NaCl, and FPIC) for sonication for 4 min (4 x (30 s ON, 30 s OFF)) (Bioruptor, Diagenode), yielding genomic DNA fragments with a bulk size of 150–500 bp. One percent of chromatin extracts were taken aside for inputs. Chromatin corresponding to 5 μg of DNA was incubated with 2 μg of anti-H3K4me3 (Diagenode; Cat#: C15410003) or anti-H3K9me3 (Diagenode; Cat#: C15410193) antibodies overnight at 4°C. The DNA-protein-antibody complexes were captured by DiaMag protein A-coated magnetic beads (Diagenode; Cat#: C03010020) by incubating at 4 °C for 2 hr. Magnetic beads were then washed with low-salt buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100, 2 mM EDTA (pH 8), 150 mM NaCl, and FPIC) and high-salt buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8), 0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100, 2 mM EDTA (pH 8), 500 mM NaCl, and FPIC). DNA was eluted with TE buffer (100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 1% SDS, 1 mM EDTA (pH 8)) from the beads overnight, and then reverse cross-linked with 1 μl of RNase A (10 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich; Cat#: R4642), followed by Proteinase K digestion (5 μl of 20 mg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich; Cat#: P2308) during 2 hr; inputs corresponding to 1% of IP were reverse cross-linked in the same conditions. DNA was purified using MinElute PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen; Cat#: 28004). Two microliters of input and ChIP were loaded on High Sensitivity D5000 ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies #5067–5592) with 2 μl of reagent (#5067–5593) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Libraries were prepared using the MicroPlex Library Preparation Kit v3 (Diagenode) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, 1–25 ng were used as input material. After adapter ligation, fragments were amplified with Illumina primers for 10 cycles. Libraries were purified using AMPure XP beads protocol (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) and quantified using the Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Library size distribution was assessed using the Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA chip (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were normalized and pooled at 2 nM and spike-in PhiX Control v3 (Illumina) was added. Sequencing was done using a NextSeq 500 instrument (Illumina) in paired-end mode (2×40 cycles) and a NextSeq 2000 instrument (Illumina) in paired-end mode (2×50 cycles). After sequencing, a primary analysis based on AOZAN software (ENS, Paris, France) (Perrin et al., 2017) was applied to demultiplex and control the quality of the raw data (based on bcl2fastq v2.20, bcl-convert v4.1.5 and FastQC modules/v0.11.5).

ChIP-seq datasets were analyzed under the Galaxy platform (https://usegalaxy.eu) (Afgan et al., 2022). The quality of raw data has been evaluated with FastQC (Galaxy Version 0.74) (https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/). Poor-quality sequences and adapters have been trimmed or removed with Trimmomatic (Galaxy Version 0.23.2) software (Bolger et al., 2014) to retain only paired reads of 40 bp with Phred score >20. Reads were mapped to the reference genome (GRCh38) using Bowtie2 (Galaxy Version 2.5.0) (Langmead et al., 2019) to generate BAM files. Duplicates were removed using the Picard tool MarkDuplicates (Galaxy Version 2.18.2.4). Narrow and broad peaks were called with MACS2 (Galaxy Version 2.2.7.1) (Feng et al., 2012) using the input as a control, FDR ≤0.05. Differential binding analysis of ChIP-Seq peak data was performed using DiffBind (Galaxy Version 2.10.0) (Ross-Innes et al., 2012). Peak annotation was performed using the ChIPseeker R package (Yu et al., 2015) and Bedtools intersect (Galaxy Version 2.28.0) (Quinlan and Hall, 2010) to annotate peaks according to their chromatin feature with genome segmentation data from ENCODE (Dunham et al., 2012; Ernst and Kellis, 2012). The Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was performed with the clusterProfiler R package (Yu et al., 2012). The significant GO categories were identified with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value ≤0.05. Data can be found under the GEO accession number GSE265792.

sec.title: Microarray
sec.p: A 6-well plate was seeded with 200,000 HeLa cells per well. The following day, cells were infected with C. trachomatis LGV L2 at MOI = 2. 24 hpi, the medium was replaced with complete medium supplemented with 5 mM DMKG or left unchanged with the addition of an equal volume of DMSO. Forty-eight hpi RNA was harvested using the RNeasy kit (Qiagen), and their quality was analyzed using the BioAnalyzer (Agilent). Transcriptome analysis was done using the GeneChip Human Transcriptome Array 2.0 in combination with the GeneChip WT PLUS Reagent kit (Applied Biosystems). 33.3 ng total RNA was used as input for the analysis that was done according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. In brief, double-stranded cDNA is first synthesized using random primers and then used as template for in vitro transcription (IVT) that produces amplified amounts of antisense mRNA (cRNA). The cRNA is used as input for a second round of first-strand cDNA synthesis, producing single-stranded sense cDNA. After fragmentation and end-labeling, the targets are hybridized to single-sample GeneChip cartridge arrays that are stained and washed on a GeneChip Fluidics Station 450 and scanned on a GeneChip scanner 3000 7 G. Cell files containing the probe cell intensity data generated by the scanner are imported into the Expression Console Software 4.0.1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for data analysis. Expression values correspond to Robust Multiarray Average (RMA) normalized probe set intensities. Data can be found under the GEO accession number GSE265791.

sec.title: RT-qPCR and qPCR
sec.p: Total RNA from cells in culture were isolated 48 hpi with the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) with DNase treatment (DNase I, Roche). RNA concentrations were determined with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and normalized to equal contents. Reverse transcription (RT) was performed using the M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase (Promega). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was undertaken on DNA or on complementary DNA (cDNA) with the LightCycler 480 system using LightCycler 480 SYBR Green Master I (Roche). Data were analyzed using the ΔΔCt method with the actin gene as a control gene (Schmittgen and Livak, 2008). Each RT-qPCR experiment was performed in duplicate and repeated at least three times. Primers used are listed in Supplementary file 7.

sec.title: tRNA quantification
sec.p: tRNAs were extracted and analyzed by northern blot as described (Torres et al., 2019) with the exception that in some cases samples were run on a 6% PAGE (instead of 8%) to get better separation between the 5 S rRNA and the U6 snRNA.

sec.title: Infection in mice
sec.p: The experiments were performed in accordance with the French national and European laws regarding the protection of animals used for experimental and other scientific purposes. The study was approved by the ethics committee of Institut Pasteur (approval N° dap210086). Female C57BL/6 J mice aged 6–7 weeks were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (France) and housed in the animal facility at Institut Pasteur. JIB-04 was synthesized as described (Wang et al., 2013). All animals were treated with 2.5 mg of medroxyprogesterone (Depo-Provera-SC, Pfizer) 7 days prior to infection to synchronize their menstrual cycle. Vaginal lavages were conducted the day prior to infection twice with 50 μl PBS each time by pipetting up and down several times, followed by swabbing to remove the mucus. On day 0, the animals were anesthetized by intramuscular injection of Ketamine/Xylazine in PBS before intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of JIB-04 (100 mg/kg body weight) resuspended in 300 μl sesame oil (Sigma #3547), control animals were injected with sesame oil only. 2×105 IFUs of C. muridarum resuspended in 5 μl of sucrose-phosphate-glutamic acid buffer (SPG: 10 mM sodium phosphate [8 mM Na2HPO4- 2 mM NaH2PO4], 220 mM sucrose, 0.50 mM l-glutamic acid) were introduced in the vagina of mice. Additional doses of JIB04 or sesame oil were injected i.p. at D2 and D4. A vaginal lavage was performed at D4 and two washes were pooled and frozen immediately in liquid nitrogen. Total RNAs and genomic DNA from lavage fluids were extracted using AllPrep DNA/RNA Micro Kit (Qiagen, #80284). At D35, the animals were sacrificed by cervical dislocation. The genital tracts were excised, imaged, and their morphology examined. Each image was segmented using Icy (https://icy.bioimageanalysis.org/) (de Chaumont et al., 2012) based on color quantization. From the binary image, a distance map and skeleton of the uterine horns were computed using the plugin Morphomath. The distance maps, corresponding to the radius of each uterus horn, were computed starting from the point of convergence of the two uterine horn skeletons.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The R environment v4.1.2 was used for analysis of tRNA quantification and RT-qPCR (R Development Core Team, 2019). Data were not averaged prior to analysis. For tRNA quantification, band intensities were measured in each well of northern blot pictures and the log2 of (band of interest intensity/control band intensity) was computed, with band of interest being either GlyGCC or ArgGCU tRNA, and with control band being either U6 or 5 S rRNA. Then, data were fitted to a mixed linear model that included the condition and the technical replicates as random covariates (i.e. band intensity ~condition + (1|replicate)). For RT-qPCR analysis, a variation of the ΔΔCt method (gene of interest versus actin) (Schmittgen and Livak, 2008) that keeps the technical replicate variations was applied. These values were fitted to a mixed linear model that included the treatment (DMSO, DMKG), the infection (Infected, Not infected) and the technical replicates as random covariates (i.e. ΔΔCt2 ~treatment * infection + (1|replicate) in Figure 5C). Contrasts were performed with the emmeans() function of the emmeans package. Statistical significance was set to p≤0.05. In each panel, type I error was controlled by correcting the p values according to the Benjamini & Hochberg method (‘BH’ option in the p.adjust() function of R). The nature of the statistical tests used in other figures are provided in the respective legend.

body.p: This is a valuable study of changes in host genome histone methylation and transcription changes associated with Chlamydia infection. boxed-text.p: Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

body.p: Thank you for submitting your article "Intracellular growth of Chlamydia trachomatis leads to global histone hypermethylation by impairing demethylation" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Dominique Soldati-Favre as the Senior Editor.
The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

This valuable study by Charendoff et al. provides interesting observations related to global histone hypermethylation in host cells, during Chlamydia trachomatis infections. The core observation they report is that the host histones are highly hypermethylated during infection, and this appears to be an amplifying effect due to continuous inhibition of demethylases, in part due to a metabolic shift in the host where succinate amounts (which inhibit demethylases) increases. The data presented are solid, however, additional data and analysis would strengthen the authors conclusions.
1) While the current data are valuable additional studies to address the mechanistic basis for methylation and transcription changes would strengthen the conclusions.

2) The strength of evidence in favor of the author's stated hypotheses varies due to unaddressed methodological hurdles and unclear experimental rationale or data interpretation as described in the reviews.

A rephrasing of interpretations is needed (cause/consequence issues) is needed. Better understanding of the metabolic impact after infection (if there is altered SAM flux, flux through the TCA cycle etc) would help the manuscript, and the effect of increased succinate (and its connection to demethylase activity) is simplistic.
1. RNA-seq analysis for Chlamydia infected cells with/without DMKG addition, Figure 6

As a conclusion drawn from the analysis of infected DEGs between the DMKG-treated and untreated populations, the authors state that "histone hypermethylation does not globally enhance nor repress the host response to infection."(line 265-266). However, the result section also states that "About one third of those (364) were no longer differentially expressed when DMKG was added to the culture medium, indicating that increasing intracellular levels of αKG during infection impacts the host cell's transcriptional response to infection (Figure 6B)."(line 238-240). Given these observations, it would be helpful to clarify how the conclusion that histone hypermethylation does not globally enhance or repress the host response to infection can be reconciled with the finding that a substantial subset of infection-induced DEGs is sensitive to DMKG treatment. In this context, further examination of the transcriptional regulatory regions of these genes-particularly by assessing the correlation between changes in H3K4me3 levels and gene expression for genes that are upregulated upon infection but reverted by DMKG-would strengthen the interpretation.
2. Chlamydia infected cell images for histone methylation Figure 1A, B

Showing only immunofluorescence images of infected cells makes it difficult to assess how histone modification states in host cells change before and after infection. Although bar graphs comparing histone modification levels between uninfected and infected cells are provided, immunofluorescence images of uninfected cells should also be included. In addition, higher-magnification images of infected cells would be helpful for better visualization. The same concern applies to Figure 1B.
3. Figure 6E

Regarding the interpretation of Figure 6E, it should be noted that the change of SAM level also effects on m6A methylation (m6A58) on tRNA which plays a role for tRNA stability, and this possibility should be discussed.
Please find below several specific comments regarding experimental rationale, data interpretation, and grammar in the manuscript.

A revised manuscript would be greatly improved by (i) the addition of experiments which more directly rule out the role of histone methylases; (ii) performing the demethylase cofactor treatment in a demethylase mutant cell line/in the presence of a dominant negative demethylase/in the presence of the JIB-04 inhibitor to assess the specificity of the effect; and by (iii) addressing the caveat that many assays (specifically, biochemical and genome-wide -omics experiments) include both cells which exhibit histone hypermethylation and those that do not, based on the heterogeneity observed in the immunofluorescent assays.
Line 24 – suggested edit: "Chromatin dynamics are…"

Line 40-41 – suggested edit: I would recommend rewriting this sentence because it gives the impression that Chlamydia does not synthesize any metabolites required for growth and instead relies entirely on the host to obtain all metabolites. (One could argue that the latter is true for any intracellular pathogen that obtains, e.g., carbon and nitrogen sources from the host, regardless of their biosynthetic capacity, thereby making this a moot point for Chlamydia. In other words, the author's statement needs clarification.)

Figure 1, Figure S1A – comment: Because the authors do not include images of an uninfected control in Figure 1, I suggest explicitly stating that the comparison of infected to uninfected cells (i.e., the plots in the lower part of Figure 1A and the images in Figure S1A) reveals that the increase in hypermethylation is specific to the infected condition. It may also be convenient to separate out the results in Figure 1A into separate panels to make referencing these results more convenient.

Figure 1, Figure S1A – comment: It seems necessary for the authors to comment on the heterogeneity of hypermethylation observed by IFA. For example, the authors report that only 10-20% of nuclei are hypermethylated in immortalized cells (though I assume this includes both infected and uninfected cells in the field – nevertheless, it seems likely to be below 50% of infected cells), whereas it appears that basically every infected cell has a brightly stained nuclei in the organoid infected with C. trachomatis (and I assume here that C. trachomatis does not grow as readily as it does in immortalized cells, raising a question as to what extent bacterial growth is the key determinant here) but the staining is very weak in cells infected with C. muridarum in the organoid, despite similar behavior to C. trachomatis in immortalized cells.

Line 88-89 – comment: If I am interpreting this sentence correctly, the authors indicate that they only detect one of the examined histone modifications in their proteomic analysis. I would suggest that the authors state in this passage that a possible reason for this is because the modifications are not present in every infected cell (i.e., the results presented in Figure 1), which would reasonably reduce the chance of detecting all modifications. I am also curious as to why H3K79 does not appear in the plot in Figure 1C (I assume this is not analogous to H3C1 K 80?).

Line 113-114 – comment: It would be helpful if the authors stated what they are comparing ciprofloxacin to, e.g., what antibiotic would have been suitable if not for its interference with host mitochondrial function and why is mitochondrial function so important here? I assume the authors intend to make a metabolic argument, but it would be good to spell this out.

Line 111-112 – comment: The authors could state more explicitly their hypothesis here before the sentence "If true…". That is, stating that they are testing whether increased bacterial replication leads to increased histone methylation. Relatedly, I wonder if the authors tested the hypothesis that bacterial protein synthesis is required for the observed phenotype. Could a short treatment of chloramphenicol ahead of the 48 h timepoint block histone hypermethylation?

Figure 3B – comment: The interpretation of these data is complicated by the fact that treatment with JIB-04 does not appear to increase histone methylation in uninfected cells and that treatment begins from a point at which histone methylation is already increased (i.e., the infected condition). In fact, it appears that the 1 µM treatment actually decreases H4K20me3 fluorescence intensity in uninfected cells. It seems it would be worth testing a broader range of concentrations or conditions to establish that the inhibitor works as expected in the uninfected control. Relatedly, that infection potentiates the effect of inhibiting histone demethylases appears to suggest the opposite of the stated hypothesis. That is, if the concentration of inhibitor is actually sufficient to inhibit demethylases in both infected and uninfected cells, then the most parsimonious explanation for the drastically increased amount of signal in infected cells treated with inhibitor would be that there is more active methylation under the untreated condition, not less demethylation.

Figure 3C – comment: I find this experiment difficult to rationalize. Would one not expect overexpression of a specific demethylase to reduce the amount of cognate methylation regardless of whether that methylation arose due to increased methylation or decreased demethylation? I find the direct measurement of demethylase activity in Figure 3D to be the most compelling evidence in favor of the author's hypothesis in this section of results, but I think that these data would be greatly enhanced by including analogous experiments that test the activity of methylases. The measurement of SAM amounts is consistent with decreased methylation, but this raises the question of how much population-level methylation activity is required to increase histone methylation late in infection, especially given the heterogeneous behavior reported in Figure 1 (that is, could reduce SAM amounts not arise from infected cells which do not exhibit hypermethylation, which appear to be the majority?). Even in individual cells in which SAM amounts are supposedly lower, is it not conceivable that the rate of methylation or the overall amount of methylation could still be dictated by methylase activity precisely because there is less demethylase activity? In other words, wouldn't lower demethylase activity enhance the ability of a lowered rate of methylation to have a meaningful effect?

Results section – "Histone hypermethylation is the result of reduced demethylase activity late in infection" – suggestion: This section of text is a single ~40-line block. I would recommend breaking it up into multiple paragraphs. This comment applies to various sections of the text.
Line 172-175 – comment: is there a literature reference to support this claim? I agree with the rationale I am just curious.
Figure 4B-C – comment: Why is a representative image not provided for the media refreshment condition in Figure 4B?

Figure S2 – suggestion: The authors should adjust the y-axis so that it does not cut off at 108 IFU/mL which gives a misleading impression of the effect size of treatment. I also question the validity of the statistics performed in Figure S2F (and presumably in all of the IFU experiments in this figure), where the data points in the two experimental groups almost entirely overlap, yet a p-value of 0.0011 is reported. The authors should double check this. The authors report using a ratio-paired t-test, but this seems like a test most suitable for a before/after experiment where the samples are actually paired, i.e. derived from the same experimental subject or biologically matched sample; it is not clear how pairing would be accomplished in the experiment as designed.

Line 192-193 – comment: I assume the authors mean "the effect of the combination [on methylation] was not tested," but it is unclear because the preceding passages refer to IFU assays where the authors did test the combination of DMKG and iron treatment (Figure S2F).
Line 197 – suggestion: "imbalance" rather than "unbalance"

Figure 5 – comment: The claim that methylation is happening "outside" H3K4me3-enriched chromatin areas suggests that there should be new, infection-specific peaks, or at least regions of increased read density, and presumably requires stronger supporting evidence than the marginal increase in genome-wide read coverage shown in Figure 5C (that is, shouldn't there be regions of the chromosome outside of peaks with measurably increased read density that are specific to infected samples? Do such regions hint at biological implications? Etc.). The authors note that the number of peaks between infected and uninfected samples are the same, which suggests that there is not a global increase in binding of methylated histones to DNA. It is hard to rationalize from these data why the authors observe cells in which immunostaining of methylated histones is greatly increased. I wonder whether the results would be different if a sorting had been applied prior to the immunoprecipitation, so as to enrich for those cells with high levels of methylated histones. As is, I think the authors need to state the caveat that these data include the many infected cells which do not exhibit increased histone methylation, at least by IFA, and that the interpretation of the data must be carried out accordingly.

Figure 3C – suggestion: The authors might consider converting these data into a heatmap to make them more legible. The plots are very small and it is a lot of information that I think would be enhanced by reorganization. At the very least both of the plots could be in a log scale to make the comparison easier. As an aside, did this analysis include a control gene which the authors did not expect to respond to infection and/or DMKG? It's not obvious to me but should be included.
Line 251 – edit: "…boost or repress…" use of "boost" here feels imprecise

Figure 6E – comment: The results with tRNA abundance are very interesting. For the assay of individual tRNA amounts, the comparison to the DMKG-treated infected sample would be helpful to establish that this behavior correlates with histone hypermethylation. I recognize this is reported for the RNA-seq data, but it raises the question of why this condition was not included when these confirmatory experiments were performed.

Line 332-334 – comment: I think the authors should reflect on this passage again; they measured demethylase activity for one histone modification in samples comparable to those in which they (i) did not robustly detect histone methylation at the proteomic level (e.g., Figure 1C) and (ii) for which they ostensibly observe only a mild increase in DNA bound to methylated histones (Figure 5). The data in Figure 3D are also normalized so as to obscure the variance in the uninfected control, which likely accentuates the measured effect from this assay. To argue from the results of this single demethylase activity experiment that cells in which there is no other strong evidence of hypermethylation are actually experiencing hypermethylation seems questionable, especially because a loss of demethylase activity could easily be accompanied by a loss in methylase activity (as indicated by the reduced amounts of SAM) and therefore a net zero change in overall methylation.

Lines 358-366 – comment: The argument the authors are making here is not entirely clear to me but seems pivotal to their rationale. I would suggest trying to revise this passage so as to emphasize the key points more clearly. For example, the authors highlight the significance of differences in an enzyme's affinity for cofactors, etc., but do not give an example of how this would explain their results. In addition, they do not explain the significance of increased GADD45A and GADD45B expression – what are these proteins? What do they do?
General comment: The authors should review the manuscript for trivial typos or grammatical errors; it would be tedious to point them out one by one – some are indicated above.
[Editors' note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Intracellular growth of Chlamydia trachomatis leads to global histone hypermethylation by impairing demethylation" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Dominique Soldati-Favre (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and two of the original reviewers.
The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that you might want to address (e.g., with clarifications in the text), as outlined below:

I think the authors have done a very careful job in their revision, and the conclusions and interpretations are better supported by the data now. This is a very interesting paper, which I strongly support for final publication.

This revised manuscript makes several important improvements over the previous version that both enhance clarity and help define the mechanistic basis. Crucially, the FRET-based SAM measurements are a helpful indication that altered metabolism of SAM is not likely to explain hypermethylation. Additional clarification and qualification of the methods and analyses help to establish the rigor of the argument being made in the manuscript. I am providing the following comments to clarify some points I raised in the original evaluation of the manuscript which may be useful for the authors to consider more thoroughly.

(1) In response to my concern about the JIB-04 treatment condition, the authors raise an important point about possible buffering of the compound's potency in the presence of competitive inhibitor iron and/or aKG. However, I do not think that this addresses the main issue, which is the question of whether the inhibitor work as expected in the authors' hands. In other words, buffering or not, if the inhibitor works, some concentration of JIB-04 should increase methylation in uninfected cells. Validating this aspect of the experiment would only strengthen the authors argument that infected cells are X-fold more sensitive to JIB-04. Moreover, the buffering argument raises the critical possibility that, if the inhibitor is working as expected, and if a metabolic/nutritional basis explains the results, then the effect of the inhibitor should be readily titrated away by the addition of iron and/or DMKG (perhaps more readily in infected vs uninfected cells). Such an experiment would provide strong evidence that demethylases specifically are responsible for the reported behaviors and is related to the following comment.

(2) The authors respond to my suggestion to demonstrate the specificity of cofactor treatment with several arguments that I am not sure address the core issue I was trying to raise. To reiterate: my suggestion was to use, e.g., dominant-negative demethylase expression, to demonstrate that the altered methylation under cofactor treatment was acting via demethylases. Because iron and a-KG are pleiotropic agents, this strikes me as an important experiment. The authors suggest the dominant negative effect of their constructs is not strong, but this would be expected under a condition where demethylase activity is already low (note that this is an interpretation of the data in favor of the authors' central argument) and the point here would be to observe a lack of response to cofactor treatment. The same logic would apply to cofactor treatment in the presence of JIB-04 inhibitor. By measuring a specific methylation mark in the presence or absence of both cofactor and dominant negative demethylase (or inhibitor), one would expect to see that the cofactor treatment would only alter methylation prevalence in the absence of the dominant negative allele (if the model is correct). The authors suggest that DMKG supplementation in the presence of JIB-04 would be difficult to interpret because both treatments slow bacterial growth (the data suggest this is a very mild growth defect), but why not use iron, which is a/the strict competitor for JIB-04 binding and which has the same effect as DMKG on methylation? Ultimately, I agree with the authors that the data demonstrating sensitivity of infected cells to JIB-04 and to DMKG and iron agree with one another and point towards a culprit (demethylases) but the suggested experiment would help establish that link causally.

(3) Regarding the rationale for overexpressing demethylases, the authors note (in response to Reviewer #2) that "we included this experiment to show that increasing the expression of one demethylase only restored demethylation of its cognate target." I would like to note that this disagrees with the rationale provided in the corresponding Results section which states: "If [the hypothesis that lysine demethylation by JmjC demethylases is low late in infection] is correct, overexpression of a given JmjC demethylase should reverse the enhanced methylation of its target residue." This is relevant to the concern I raised about this experiment, which I am not sure is fully addressed by the authors' response. Specifically, I was concerned with the notion that this experiment addresses the hypothesis that is stated in the manuscript, because demethylase overexpression should reduce cognate methylation no matter the source of methylation. If, by contrast, the rationale for this experiment is to show that hypermethylation is reversible when enough demethylase activity is present, then I have no major issue with the experiment. But I would emphasize that I think this is a very different interpretation from the one offered in the Results section which implies that this experiment addresses whether hypermethylation is caused by low demethylase activity late in infection. (Note that this interpretation is explicitly stated again in the same paragraph of the Results section after the data are described.) It also appears to be at odds with the notion that there is a metabolic/cofactor limitation on demethylase activity if simply expressing more demethylase (which requires cofactor) is sufficient to reverse hypermethylation. Is demethylase gene expression reduced during infection?

(4) With respect to the point raised about Figure 6C, I would like to clarify that while I may be mistaken about whether the data are in logarithmic scale, clearly the data are computing two different kinds of fold change, one that produces negative fold-changes (the microarray data – negative fold-change being usually accomplished by log transformation), and one that does not (the RT-qPCR data, which is reported as values >0). Why not be consistent here for the sake of comparison and legibility of the figure? I did not raise an issue about microarray versus RT-qPCR, I raised an issue about being able to easily interpret the data. Of course, this was simply a suggestion, and the authors may do as they wish. Finally, I raised a point about a control gene. By this I did not mean a normalization gene (which does not guarantee that its expression is unchanged unless validated empirically!) but rather a gene which the microarray data suggests is not changed by treatment and/or infection which can be confirmed by RT-qPCR identically to the other genes in this figure (i.e., using ACTN as normalization). This is typically a good internal control for any such analysis specifically because changes in RT-qPCR data can arise due to changes in the expression of a normalization gene and other artifacts.

1. RNA-seq analysis for Chlamydia infected cells with/without DMKG addition, Figure 6

As a conclusion drawn from the analysis of infected DEGs between the DMKG-treated and untreated populations, the authors state that "histone hypermethylation does not globally enhance nor repress the host response to infection."(line 265-266).
